linear-transformations-s1.title: A square and its image
linear-transformations-s1.text: A linear transformation $T$ sends the unit square (dashed) to the shaded parallelogram. The arrows show $T(\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle)$ and $T(\left\langle 0, 1 \right\rangle)$.

linear-transformations-s2.title: A transformation given by a rule

why.correct: The columns are the images: $T(\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle) = \left\langle 2, 1 \right\rangle$ and $T(\left\langle 0, 1 \right\rangle) = \left\langle -1, 1 \right\rangle$.
options: The images were written as rows; they go in as columns.
The columns are in the wrong order: the image of the first unit vector comes first.
$T(\left\langle 0, 1 \right\rangle) = \left\langle -1, 1 \right\rangle$, so the bottom right entry is $1$.
This uses the images as rows instead of columns.
This multiplies matching entries; use row times column.

items.q: What is the area of the shaded parallelogram?

mistakes.why: The area is the determinant $ad - bc$, not a sum of entries.

why.correct: The unit square (area $1$) is scaled by $\det \left[ \begin{matrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{matrix} \right] = 2 + 1 = 3$.

items.q: A triangle of area $5$ is transformed by $T$. What is the area of its image?

mistakes.why: $3$ is the scale factor; multiply the area $5$ by it.
Areas are multiplied by $\det T = 3$, not increased by $3$.

items.q: Does $T$ flip the plane over, reversing orientation?
options: Yes: it sends a vector to the left of the $y$-axis
Yes: one entry of its matrix is negative

why.correct: A flip shows up as a negative determinant. $\det T = 3 > 0$, so orientation is kept.
options: Moving some vectors left is not a flip; rotations do that too.
Single entries do not decide it; the sign of the determinant does.

why.correct: Row 1 holds the coefficients of $x + 2y$; row 2 those of $3x - y$.
options: Coefficients of each output, row by row.
This puts the first output's coefficients in a column.
The coefficient of $y$ in $3x - y$ is $-1$.
The coefficient of $x$ comes first in each row.
Apply the rule; the input is $(1, 1)$.

why.correct: Solve $x + 2y = 4$ and $3x - y = 5$: from the second, $y = 3x - 5$; then $x + 6x - 10 = 4$, so $x = 2$ and $y = 1$. Check: $L(\left\langle 2, 1 \right\rangle) = \left\langle 4, 5 \right\rangle$.
options: $L(\left\langle 4, 5 \right\rangle) = \left\langle 14, 7 \right\rangle$; the output is not its own input.
This is $L(\left\langle 4, 5 \right\rangle)$, an output, not the input.

items.q: What does $L$ do to areas and orientation?
options: Multiplies areas by $7$ and reverses orientation
Multiplies areas by $7$ and keeps orientation
Multiplies areas by $5$ and keeps orientation

why.correct: $\det = 1(-1) - 2(3) = -7$. Areas are multiplied by $\left| -7 \right| = 7$, and the negative sign means a flip.
options: Areas are positive; use the absolute value.

items.q: Which matrix rotates the plane by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ counterclockwise?

why.correct: A quarter turn counterclockwise sends $\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle$ to $\left\langle 0, 1 \right\rangle$ and $\left\langle 0, 1 \right\rangle$ to $\left\langle -1, 0 \right\rangle$: those are the columns.
options: Columns: images of the two unit vectors.
This sends $\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle$ to $\left\langle 0, -1 \right\rangle$: a clockwise quarter turn.
This is the reflection across the $x$-axis.
This is a half turn, by $\pi$.

items.q: Which matrix reflects the plane across the line $y = x$?

why.correct: The reflection swaps the coordinates: $\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle \to \left\langle 0, 1 \right\rangle$ and $\left\langle 0, 1 \right\rangle \to \left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle$.

items.q: What is the image of $\left\langle 2, 0 \right\rangle$ under a rotation by $\frac{\pi}{6}$ counterclockwise?
Rotate $\left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle$ by $\frac{\pi}{4}$ counterclockwise. What is the second component of the image?

why.correct: $\left[ \begin{matrix} \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{matrix} \right]\left[ \begin{matrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 \\ \sqrt{2} \end{matrix} \right]$: the vector at angle $\frac{\pi}{4}$ turns to point straight up.

items.q: Why is $S(\left\langle x, y \right\rangle) = \left\langle x + 1, y \right\rangle$ not a linear transformation?
options: $S(\left\langle 0, 0 \right\rangle) = \left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle$, but a linear transformation keeps the origin fixed
It slides each point the same way, which a matrix can do

why.correct: Any matrix times $\left[ \begin{matrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right]$ is $\left[ \begin{matrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix} \right]$. Here the origin moves to $(1, 0)$, so no matrix gives $S$.
options: The origin moves; a matrix cannot do that.
Leaving $y$ alone is fine; the reflection across the $y$-axis does too.
A slide moves the origin, which no matrix can do.
Sending $\left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle$ to $\left\langle 2, 0 \right\rangle$ is allowed; a stretch does it.

items.q: The shear $\left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right]$ is applied to $\left\langle x, 2 \right\rangle$. Write the first component of the image.

mistakes.why: Multiply the $3$ by the second component, $2$.

items.q: Under the dilation $\left[ \begin{matrix} k & 0 \\ 0 & k \end{matrix} \right]$, $k$ is increased from $2$ to $3$. Predict each change.

variables.name: The area of the image of the unit square
variables.why: The area is $\det = k^2$, which grows from $4$ to $9$.

variables.name: The direction of the image of $\left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle$
variables.why: The image is $\left\langle k, k \right\rangle$, a longer arrow pointing the same way for any positive $k$.

why.correct: A dilation stretches every vector by $k$ without turning it.
